patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral eyelid drooping of decades duration initially diagnosed as chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia — now worsening with new fatigability
patient.hpi:
A 53-year-old Ghanaian woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the neurology clinic for evaluation of worsening bilateral eyelid ptosis and increasing generalized fatigue. She first noticed left upper eyelid drooping at approximately age 20, which gradually worsened over years and was eventually followed by bilateral ptosis. She reported no diplopia, diurnal variation, dysphagia, or other muscle weakness throughout this time. She had multiple prior evaluations, and the consistent clinical picture — gradual onset without fatigability, no diplopia, absent ice pack test response at initial evaluation — led to a clinical diagnosis of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO).

Over the past 8 months, however, she noticed new and different symptoms: significant fatigue with prolonged talking or chewing, muffled voice quality that was worse in the afternoon, and difficulty completing her usual 30-minute walk due to bilateral leg fatigue. She also experienced occasional choking with liquids. Crucially, she noted for the first time that the eyelid drooping seemed more pronounced when tired and somewhat better in the morning — a pattern she had not observed before. She also reported a sensation of double images on lateral gaze, which resolved with eye closure.

Her ocular history included bilateral elevated intraocular pressures (managed with timolol eye drops) and bilateral cataract surgery 3 years prior (significant improvement in acuity post-operatively). She had no family history of neuromuscular or mitochondrial disease. On examination, complete bilateral ptosis was present. The ice pack test produced a 4 mm improvement bilaterally, which was POSITIVE — in contrast to prior documented negative result. Restricted extraocular movements were present, more pronounced in vertical gaze. A new finding was fatigable palate elevation on the SLURP test, absent in prior evaluations.

physical_exam.general: Well-appearing middle-aged woman; alert and cooperative; bilateral ptosis visible immediately
physical_exam.neurological: Complete bilateral ptosis (left > right). Positive ice pack test (4 mm improvement bilaterally in 5 minutes). Extraocular movements restricted in all directions, more so in vertical gaze; no ophthalmoplegia pain. Diplopia elicitable on extreme lateral gaze but not in primary position. Cerebellar examination normal. Sensation intact throughout. Gait normal.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs
physical_exam.abdomen: Soft; mild central adiposity; no organomegaly
physical_exam.extremities: No edema; bilateral posterior subcapsular lens opacity noted by patient (post-cataract surgery)

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis, presenting as long-standing 'ocular' disease previously misdiagnosed as chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia

differential.key_features: Decades-long ophthalmoplegia is suggestive; mitochondrial genetic panel and muscle biopsy if diagnostic doubt persists; AChR positive here favors MG.
KSS includes pigmentary retinopathy and cardiac conduction disease; ECG and ophthalmology examination clarify.
OPMD is hereditary, family history relevant; PABPN1 genetic testing.
Decades-long ocular presentation incompatible with LEMS.
No proptosis, lid retraction; no Graves history.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR antibody positive; TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 2-3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder
Increased jitter and blocking on extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi confirms NMJ transmission failure

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No thymoma; thymic involution appropriate for age

optimal_actions.action: Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

tool_parameters.query: myasthenia gravis MGFA classification treatment thymectomy

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for MG-exacerbating agents (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, procainamide)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Flag aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, telithromycin, NMBs as contraindicated or use-with-caution in MG

optimal_actions.action: Bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) — repeat q4h in crisis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline FVC/NIF to assess crisis risk in patients with bulbar or limb involvement

optimal_actions.action: Bedside ice-pack test for ptosis (cheap, ~80% sensitive for ocular MG)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Improvement of ptosis after 2 minutes of cooling supports MG

optimal_actions.action: Consider mitochondrial genetic panel and/or muscle biopsy if AChR positivity does not fully resolve diagnostic doubt
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mitochondrial mutations would support CPEO; muscle biopsy ragged-red fibers / COX-negative fibers

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: Confirm AChR antibody positivity — overturns CPEO label
RNS and SFEMG to confirm NMJ pathology
Therapeutic trial of pyridostigmine with objective documentation of improvement
Ophthalmology and patient education on revised diagnosis
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Long-standing 'CPEO' labels are not infrequently revised to ocular MG when fatigability emerges or serology becomes positive.
Mitochondrial workup is OPTIONAL only — pursue if AChR negative or treatment response poor.

red_herrings.data_point: Prior diagnosis of CPEO (chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Accept the CPEO label and pursue mitochondrial workup; miss MG.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Emerging fatigability and positive AChR antibodies overturn the CPEO label — diagnostic re-anchoring is essential.

red_herrings.data_point: Prior CPEO diagnosis over 30 years — anchoring bias
red_herrings.intended_effect: Long-standing prior diagnosis creates anchoring bias toward continuing the CPEO label despite new clinical features
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Positive ice pack test + new fatigability + AChR antibody = MG; prior CPEO diagnosis was incorrect

red_herrings.data_point: Borderline lactate/pyruvate ratio suggesting possible mitochondrial disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Borderline L/P ratio with CPEO history increases suspicion for mitochondrial myopathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Serum lactate is normal; borderline L/P ratio is non-specific; definitive AChR antibody supersedes mitochondrial concern

red_herrings.data_point: Timolol eye drops as incidental medication
red_herrings.intended_effect: Topical medications often overlooked; timolol seems innocuous for ocular hypertension management
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Topical timolol has systemic absorption and is contraindicated in MG — may have been exacerbating disease for years

output.interpretation: AChR binding antibody markedly elevated at 5.8 nmol/L (reference < 0.4 nmol/L). AChR blocking antibody positive. Anti-MuSK antibody negative. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are found in a subset of patients with neuromuscular junction disorders; an elevated result supports but is not exclusive to myasthenia gravis
abnormal_values_summary: AChR binding antibody 5.8 nmol/L (ref <0.4 nmol/L) — markedly elevated

findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG — ORBICULARIS OCULI

Indication: Evaluation of bilateral ptosis

RESULTS:
  MCD: 58 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
  Blocking: 18% of potential pairs
  Fiber density: 2.1 (mildly elevated, borderline)

IMPRESSION: Markedly increased mean consecutive difference with 18% blocking, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Mildly elevated fiber density is a borderline finding. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: SFEMG (orbicularis oculi): MCD 58 µs with 18% blocking — markedly increased jitter consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

Indication: Neuromuscular junction evaluation

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS, orbicularis oculi, nasalis, deltoid

RESULTS:
  Orbicularis oculi: Decrement 16% [>10% abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Nasalis: Decrement 13% ABNORMAL
  Deltoid (proximal): Decrement 11% ABNORMAL

IMPRESSION: Abnormal decremental response at 3 Hz in cranial and proximal limb muscles, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.summary: CPEO vs MG: ice pack test, fatigability, and AChR antibody are key distinguishing features; beta-blocker topical agents reported to affect NMJ transmission.

interactions:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — TIMOLOL (OPHTHALMIC) AND NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION DISORDERS

Query: Beta-blocker timolol (ophthalmic) in patients with disorders of neuromuscular transmission

FINDINGS:
  TIMOLOL (topical beta-blocker):
  - Systemic absorption occurs with topical ophthalmic administration (~60-70% via nasolacrimal duct)
  - Beta-blockers have been reported to impair neuromuscular transmission in susceptible patients
  - Multiple case reports describe worsening of neuromuscular junction disease with topical beta-blocker use
  - Beta-blockers are generally used with caution in conditions affecting NMJ function
  - Effect is dose-dependent; 0.5% timolol BID achieves measurable systemic levels

  ALTERNATIVES WITHOUT REPORTED NMJ EFFECTS:
  - Prostaglandin analogs (e.g., latanoprost 0.005% once daily)
  - Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., dorzolamide 2% BID)
warnings: Timolol (ophthalmic): systemic absorption reported; beta-blockers associated with NMJ transmission impairment in susceptible patients; prostaglandin analogs and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are alternatives.
